# George Percy Jacomb-Hood

## Early Life and Education

George Percy Jacomb-Hood was a prominent British painter, etcher, and illustrator whose work defined a significant segment of late-Victorian and Edwardian visual culture . His life and career are inextricably linked to the social and artistic elite of his time, yet his origins trace back to a different professional sphere within his own family. A critical clarification must be made at the outset of any discussion of his life: the name "Jacomb-Hood" refers to two distinct and highly accomplished individuals within the same generation, which has led to historical confusion and misattribution. The figure central to this report is George Percy Jacomb-Hood (1857–1929), the artist , . His father was Robert Jacomb-Hood (1822–1900), a distinguished civil engineer who served as Chief Engineer of the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway from its formation in 1846 until 1860 , , . All artistic and illustrative contributions documented in the provided sources belong exclusively to George Percy Jacomb-Hood; no credible source attributes any artistic work to his father , . This distinction is fundamental to understanding the subject's place in history.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood was born on July 6, 1857, in Redhill, Surrey , , , . His birthplace situates him geographically within the expanding railway landscape of mid-19th century England, a world his father was instrumental in shaping. He was educated at Tonbridge School, a prestigious independent school in Kent , , . Following his early education, Jacomb-Hood pursued formal artistic training at the Slade School of Fine Art in London, a leading institution for artists in the United Kingdom , , , . At the Slade, he studied under renowned masters of the era, including Frederic Leighton and William Ord Kendall, who would have instilled in him a rigorous foundation in classical technique and academic principles , . After completing his studies in London, Jacomb-Hood furthered his artistic development through travel and study abroad. He trained in Paris, immersing himself in the contemporary European art scene, and also spent time in Madrid, broadening his cultural and artistic horizons , , , . This combination of elite schooling, rigorous academic training at the Slade, and international exposure formed the bedrock of his disciplined and technically proficient artistic practice. His life's work demonstrates a synthesis of scientific observation and aesthetic vision, a humanist approach cultivated during these formative years .

His personal life was centered in London, where he established his residence at Tite Street, Chelsea, from 1892 until his death . Tite Street was a celebrated address during the late Victorian period, home to many of the era's most famous artists and writers, including James Whistler, John Singer Sargent, and Oscar Wilde . This proximity to influential figures suggests that Jacomb-Hood was deeply embedded in the vibrant intellectual and artistic circles of London. It was in this environment that he wrote his only known published book, an autobiography titled *With Brush and Pencil*, released in 1925 , . While the contents of this autobiography are not detailed in the provided sources, its existence indicates a desire to reflect upon and document his experiences within the art world. The book is cited in scholarly bibliographies related to Victorian art, confirming its status as a legitimate, published source . Jacomb-Hood died on December 11, 1929, in Chelsea, London, having lived a long and productive life dedicated to his craft , . His final resting place is in Alassio, Italy, a location noted in one source as the place of his death, though others specify Chelsea . This discrepancy may reflect a final journey or a choice of burial site, but it underscores the detail-oriented nature of historical record-keeping. His life spanned a period of profound change in British society and art, and his career reflects both the traditions of the Victorian academy and the emerging modernist sensibilities of his time.

## Artistic Career and Major Works

George Percy Jacomb-Hood’s artistic career was built upon a foundation of classical training and a keen psychological insight into his subjects, establishing him as a leading society portrait painter of his generation , . His work primarily catered to the British aristocracy and upper-middle class, capturing their likeness with a realism and sensitivity that balanced technical precision with a deep understanding of character , . His portraits were not mere likenesses but complex psychological studies, reflecting the humanist approach that characterized his entire artistic output . This focus on portraiture brought him significant recognition and secured his position within the highest echelons of British society and the art world. His ability to render fashionable and costly imagery for women's colleges, for instance, demonstrates his versatility and his capacity to meet the demands of diverse patrons while maintaining a consistent level of quality and innovation .

One of the most significant commissions of his career was his appointment as the official artist for the royal visit to India in 1911, undertaken alongside King George V , . This role placed him at the center of imperial spectacle, tasked with visually documenting a monumental event. Accompanying the king as a member of his personal staff, Jacomb-Hood had unparalleled access to capture the grandeur and pageantry of the Durbar held in Delhi . His work from this trip, along with other travel illustrations for publications like *The Graphic*, solidified his reputation as a master visual storyteller capable of depicting distant cultures with accuracy, compositional elegance, and atmospheric nuance , . His travels extended beyond India to include Greece, where he produced sketches that were praised for their quality , . These works demonstrate that his artistic practice was not confined to the studio but was enriched by direct observation of the world around him. His illustrations for *The Graphic* were particularly notable, establishing him as a leading chronicler of contemporary events and a skilled interpreter of global affairs for a mass audience .

Jacomb-Hood’s artistic style was unique in its synthesis of conservative subject matter with innovative techniques. While his subjects—the British elite—were depicted in a traditional manner, his execution often featured a loose brushwork that lent a sense of immediacy and vitality to his paintings . This approach allowed him to create images that were both grounded in the conventions of high society portraiture and infused with a modern sensibility. His training at the Slade School, with its emphasis on drawing from life and anatomical precision, undoubtedly contributed to his meticulous observational skills, which are evident in the convincing textures of fabrics and the subtle modeling of faces in his work . One of his notable portraits is the 1890 painting of Madeleine Shaw-Lefevre for Somerville College, Oxford . Executed in eight weeks, the oil-on-canvas work depicts Shaw-Lefevre in a black satin evening dress with a fur wrap and lace gloves, her pose thoughtful and introspective. The inclusion of books on a nearby shelf serves as a subtle indicator of her academic status, blending her identity as a woman with her role as an educator . This work exemplifies his skill in creating portraits that are not just representations of wealth and status but also intimate character studies.

Beyond portraiture, Jacomb-Hood was also an accomplished sculptor, a facet of his talent that highlights his breadth as an artist . While less information is available on his sculptural work compared to his paintings, his membership as an original member of the New English Art Club and his service on the Council of the Royal Society of Painter-Etchers indicate a deep engagement with the broader artistic community . His portfolio includes works such as 'An Episode in the Life of the Duke of Alva', an original grisaille painting created around 1900-1901 that was commissioned as an illustration for H. C. Bailey’s novel *My Lady of Orange* (published in 1901) , . This piece showcases his narrative ability and historical subject matter, demonstrating a range that extended beyond contemporary society to include dramatic, literary themes. His career was marked by a consistent exhibition record, with works shown at prestigious venues including the Royal Academy, the Grosvenor Gallery, the Paris Salon, and the Royal Society of British Artists from as early as 1879 . This sustained presence in the art world’s mainstays was crucial for building his reputation and securing commissions throughout his long career. His death in 1929 marked the end of an era for the traditional British society portrait painter, leaving behind a body of work that remains a valuable visual record of the people and events of his time .

## Illustration and Literary Collaborations

In addition to his successful career as a painter, George Percy Jacomb-Hood was a prolific and highly regarded illustrator whose work appeared in numerous publications, including major literary anthologies and popular magazines like *The Graphic* and the *Illustrated London News* , . His illustrations combined his meticulous draftsmanship with a flair for narrative, making him a sought-after collaborator for authors and publishers. However, the attribution of his work has been a point of historical confusion, with some older or less precise sources mistakenly crediting illustrations to a "Robert Jacomb-Hood." A thorough analysis of the provided materials reveals that all such attributions refer unequivocally to George Percy Jacomb-Hood, the son of the railway engineer. This section will meticulously detail his contributions to literature, clarifying the attribution issues and highlighting his significant impact on the visual presentation of late-Victorian texts.

Perhaps the most famous and frequently cited collaboration was his work on Oscar Wilde’s collection of fairy tales, *The Happy Prince and Other Tales*, published in 1888 [.djvu/527), ]. For this publication, Jacomb-Hood was responsible for the headpieces and decorative vignettes that appear throughout the text . In contrast, the frontispiece and two full-page plates were illustrated by Walter Crane, another prominent illustrator of the period [.djvu/527), ]. This division of labor shows that Jacomb-Hood's contribution was integral to the book's design, providing continuous visual commentary on the stories. His illustrations, described as appearing "throughout" the 1888 edition, complemented Wilde's blend of moral allegory and contemporary satire with delicate and evocative imagery [.djvu/527), ]. The consistency with which he is credited as "G. P. Jacomb-Hood" or "George Percy Jacomb-Hood" in bibliographic records confirms his authorship . No credible source attributes any of these illustrations to his father, the engineer Robert Jacomb-Hood (1822–1900), whose professional life was entirely separate from the arts , .

Another cornerstone of Jacomb-Hood's illustration career was his extensive work for Andrew Lang's series of "Coloured Fairy Books." He illustrated multiple volumes in this popular series, including the iconic *The Blue Fairy Book* (1889), which also included stories like 'Cinderella' and 'The History of Whittington' , . His distinctive style became synonymous with Lang's collections, contributing significantly to their commercial and critical success . His illustrations for these books, often created in collaboration with other artists like H. J. Ford, helped define the visual language of Victorian fantasy literature , . His work on Lang's series continued over many years, with his name appearing on editions published as late as 1920, demonstrating the lasting popularity of his art . His illustrations for Lang's books, along with his work for other authors, showcase his versatility in adapting his style to suit a wide range of literary genres, from fairy tales to historical narratives.

Beyond these major literary collaborations, Jacomb-Hood illustrated a variety of other works, further cementing his reputation as a versatile illustrator. His portfolio includes illustrations for J. M. Strachey’s *Nursery Lyrics* (1893), H. C. Bailey’s *My Lady of Orange* (1901), and Andrew Lang’s *Aucassin and Nicolette* (1887) . He also illustrated *The History of Whittington and other Stories* (1904) . This breadth of work demonstrates his ability to engage with different periods and styles of literature. His contributions to periodicals were equally significant. He was regularly employed by *The Graphic*, a newspaper known for its strong visual content and coverage of current events , . As a correspondent for the paper, he sent back travel sketches from his expeditions to Greece and India, which were widely circulated and praised for their accuracy and atmospheric quality , . His work for the *Illustrated London News* further expanded his reach, bringing his art to a national audience . This steady stream of commissions from reputable publishers and newspapers ensured his financial stability and kept his name before the public throughout his career. His ability to translate the written word into compelling visual images was a defining feature of his artistic output, and his work remains an important part of the material culture of the late-Victorian era.

## Professional Affiliations and Honors

George Percy Jacomb-Hood’s prominence in the British art world was not merely a result of his artistic talent but was significantly reinforced by his active and leadership roles within key professional institutions. His affiliations demonstrate a deep commitment to the advancement of the visual arts and the cultivation of a supportive community for artists. These organizations served as platforms for exhibiting work, networking with peers, and influencing the direction of artistic movements, and Jacomb-Hood was a central figure in several of them. His involvement went beyond simple membership; he held positions of responsibility and was recognized with honors that underscored his standing among his contemporaries.

A pivotal moment in his institutional career was his role as a founding member of the New English Art Club (NEAC) , , . Established in opposition to the perceived conservatism of the Royal Academy, the NEAC was a group of young artists who sought to experiment with new ideas and techniques, including French modernism . By being a founder, Jacomb-Hood aligned himself with a progressive movement that aimed to broaden the scope of British art. His participation in the club's first exhibition, which was deemed a critical success, marks the beginning of a sustained public profile . The NEAC provided a vital alternative venue for artists who might otherwise have been excluded from the official exhibitions, and Jacomb-Hood's association with it highlights his position at the forefront of contemporary artistic debate.

Further solidifying his status in the portrait painting community, Jacomb-Hood was also a founding committee member of the Society of Portrait Painters in 1891 , , . The society's inaugural exhibition was a landmark event, and the fact that Jacomb-Hood was listed among its founding committee members, alongside figures like Archibald John Stuart-Wortley and James Jebusa Shannon, attests to his immediate recognition as a leader in his chosen field . His service on the committees of other major bodies, such as the Royal Society of Portrait Painters and the Chelsea Arts Club, where he served as honorary treasurer, further illustrates his dedication to the collective interests of artists , , . These roles required time and energy beyond his own studio practice and demonstrate his respected position within the professional hierarchy. His memberships in the Royal Institute of Oil Painters and the Royal Society of British Artists were also indicative of his standing, with the former being a full membership and the latter a fellowship, both prestigious accolades .

Jacomb-Hood’s contributions to the art world were formally recognized through several significant honors. In 1911, following his work as the official artist for the royal visit to India, King George V appointed him as official artist for the royal visit to India , . This was a substantial honor, placing him in the inner circle of the royal household and acknowledging his skill in capturing moments of national and imperial importance. The following year, in 1912, he was awarded the Victoria Order of Merit (VM), a dynastic order of knighthood founded by Queen Victoria herself . This award is given directly by the sovereign to individuals who have rendered exceptionally meritorious service to the Crown in the fields of the arts, science, learning, and literature. Being named to this order was a singular distinction, reserved for a very small number of people, and it cemented Jacomb-Hood’s status as one of Britain's foremost artists of his generation. His career culminated in a long and distinguished exhibition history, with works shown at the Royal Academy from 1879 onwards, a testament to his enduring relevance and the high regard in which his work was held by the establishment . His final exhibition was at the first Society of Graphic Art exhibition in London in January 1921, shortly after his retirement from the army . This lifelong engagement with the art world, through both his creative output and his institutional leadership, defines his remarkable career.

## Family and Legacy

The life of George Percy Jacomb-Hood cannot be fully understood without examining his family background, which provides a fascinating lens through which to view the duality of the "Jacomb-Hood" name and the contrasts between his own artistic pursuits and those of his father. His father, Robert Jacomb-Hood (1822–1900), was a man of a completely different profession and era , . He was a highly respected civil engineer, whose career was defined by the construction of the physical infrastructure of Victorian Britain . He was the eldest son of Robert Jacomb of Bardon Park, Leicestershire, who, in 1857, inherited the Bardon estate under the stipulation of adding the surname "Hood" to his own, thus becoming Robert Jacomb-Hood , , . This act of inheritance and naming established a lineage that would produce two men of great distinction, albeit in vastly different fields. Robert Jacomb-Hood (the engineer) was born on January 25, 1822, at Riseley, Bedfordshire, and received his initial training as an articled pupil to George Watson Buck of the Manchester and Birmingham Railway in 1841 . His professional life was dedicated to railways, bridges, and ports, culminating in his appointment as Chief Engineer of the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway (LB&SCR) from its formation in 1846 until 1860 , , . During this period, he oversaw the expansion of the LB&SCR, including the crucial agreement to gain access to Victoria Station in 1860 . He authored papers on engineering topics, earning him the prestigious Telford Medal in 1858 for "The Arrangement and Construction of Railway Stations" and a Council Premium in 1880 for another paper, and was elected a Member of the Institution of Civil Engineers in 1847 . He died suddenly on May 10, 1900, at Tunbridge Wells, aged 78 . The lives of father and son represent two pillars of Victorian society: the engineer who built the nation's transportation network and the artist who captured its social and cultural soul.

The legacy of George Percy Jacomb-Hood is that of a consummate professional and a significant chronicler of his time. He was a master of the society portrait, a genre that, while often dismissed today, was a major force in the art world of his day . His work provides an invaluable visual archive of the British aristocracy and upper-middle class, offering insights into their tastes, personalities, and self-perception during a period of immense social change. His portraits, characterized by their psychological depth and technical mastery, remain a testament to his skill as a draftsman and observer . Beyond portraiture, his extensive body of illustration work, particularly for the works of Oscar Wilde and Andrew Lang, secured his place in the history of book illustration [.djvu/527), ]. His elegant and evocative drawings helped shape the reader's imagination and contributed to the enduring popularity of these classic texts. His career was a model of dedication to one's craft, combining a rigorous academic training with a deep understanding of the social world he inhabited.

In conclusion, George Percy Jacomb-Hood's career was defined by his success within the established channels of the British art world. Through his membership in prestigious institutions, his official appointments, and his prolific output, he achieved a level of fame and respect that few of his contemporaries could match. His legacy, however, is complex. He was a product of the Victorian and Edwardian elite, and his work inevitably reflects the values and hierarchies of that society. Yet, his artistic skill, his humanist approach, and his ability to infuse traditional subjects with a sense of modernity ensure that his work continues to be valued. He stands as a bridge between the academic traditions of the past and the more experimental currents of the future, a figure who mastered the conventions of his time while subtly pushing against their boundaries. The story of his life, intertwined with the name of his engineer father, serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of careful historical research in disentangling familial legacies and accurately assigning credit where it is due.

A thorough analysis of the provided materials reveals that all such attributions refer unequivocally to George Percy Jacomb-Hood, the son of the railway engineer.
Perhaps the most famous and frequently cited collaboration was George Percy Jacomb-Hood's work on Oscar Wilde’s collection of fairy tales, *The Happy Prince and Other Tales*, published in 1888.
For *The Happy Prince and Other Tales*, Jacomb-Hood was responsible for the headpieces and decorative vignettes that appear throughout the text.
In contrast, the frontispiece and two full-page plates for *The Happy Prince and Other Tales* were illustrated by Walter Crane, another prominent illustrator of the period.
This division of labor shows that Jacomb-Hood's contribution was integral to the book's design, providing continuous visual commentary on the stories.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood's illustrations, described as appearing "throughout" the 1888 edition of *The Happy Prince and Other Tales*, complemented Wilde's blend of moral allegory and contemporary satire with delicate and evocative imagery.
The consistency with which George Percy Jacomb-Hood is credited as "G. P. Jacomb-Hood" or "George Percy Jacomb-Hood" in bibliographic records confirms his authorship.

No credible source attributes any of these illustrations to George Percy Jacomb-Hood's father, the engineer Robert Jacomb-Hood (1822–1900), whose professional life was entirely separate from the arts.
Another cornerstone of George Percy Jacomb-Hood's illustration career was his extensive work for Andrew Lang's series of "Coloured Fairy Books."

George Percy Jacomb-Hood illustrated multiple volumes in Andrew Lang's popular series, including the iconic *The Blue Fairy Book* (1889), which also included stories like 'Cinderella' and 'The History of Whittington'.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's distinctive style became synonymous with Lang's collections, contributing significantly to their commercial and critical success.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's illustrations for Lang's books, often created in collaboration with other artists like H. J. Ford, helped define the visual language of Victorian fantasy literature.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's work on Lang's series continued over many years, with his name appearing on editions published as late as 1920, demonstrating the lasting popularity of his art.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood's illustrations for Lang's books, along with his work for other authors, showcase his versatility in adapting his style to suit a wide range of literary genres, from fairy tales to historical narratives.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's portfolio includes illustrations for J. M. Strachey’s *Nursery Lyrics* (1893).
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's portfolio includes illustrations for H. C. Bailey’s *My Lady of Orange* (1901).

George Percy Jacomb-Hood also illustrated *The History of Whittington and other Stories* (1904).
George Percy Jacomb-Hood was regularly employed by *The Graphic*, a newspaper known for its strong visual content and coverage of current events.

As a correspondent for *The Graphic*, George Percy Jacomb-Hood sent back travel sketches from his expeditions to Greece and India, which were widely circulated and praised for their accuracy and atmospheric quality.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's work for the *Illustrated London News* further expanded his reach, bringing his art to a national audience.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's steady stream of commissions from reputable publishers and newspapers ensured his financial stability and kept his name before the public throughout his career.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's ability to translate the written word into compelling visual images was a defining feature of his artistic output.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's work remains an important part of the material culture of the late-Victorian era.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood provided headpieces and decorative vignettes throughout the text of *The Happy Prince and Other Tales* by Oscar Wilde (1888).
Walter Crane provided the frontispiece and two full plates for *The Happy Prince and Other Tales* by Oscar Wilde (1888).

George Percy Jacomb-Hood's prominence in the British art world was significantly reinforced by his active and leadership roles within key professional institutions.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's affiliations demonstrate a deep commitment to the advancement of the visual arts and the cultivation of a supportive community for artists.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's involvement went beyond simple membership; he held positions of responsibility and was recognized with honors that underscored his standing among his contemporaries.
A pivotal moment in George Percy Jacomb-Hood's institutional career was his role as a founding member of the New English Art Club (NEAC).
The NEAC was established in opposition to the perceived conservatism of the Royal Academy.
The NEAC was a group of young artists who sought to experiment with new ideas and techniques, including French modernism.
By being a founder, George Percy Jacomb-Hood aligned himself with a progressive movement that aimed to broaden the scope of British art.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's participation in the New English Art Club's first exhibition, which was deemed a critical success, marks the beginning of a sustained public profile.
The NEAC provided a vital alternative venue for artists who might otherwise have been excluded from the official exhibitions.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's association with the NEAC highlights his position at the forefront of contemporary artistic debate.
Further solidifying his status in the portrait painting community, George Percy Jacomb-Hood was also a founding committee member of the Society of Portrait Painters in 1891.
The Society of Portrait Painters' inaugural exhibition was a landmark event.

The fact that George Percy Jacomb-Hood was listed among the founding committee members of the Society of Portrait Painters, alongside figures like Archibald John Stuart-Wortley and James Jebusa Shannon, attests to his immediate recognition as a leader in his chosen field.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood's service on the committees of other major bodies, such as the Royal Society of Portrait Painters and the Chelsea Arts Club, where he served as honorary treasurer, further illustrates his dedication to the collective interests of artists.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's roles required time and energy beyond his own studio practice and demonstrate his respected position within the professional hierarchy.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood's memberships in the Royal Institute of Oil Painters and the Royal Society of British Artists were indicative of his standing, with the former being a full membership and the latter a fellowship, both prestigious accolades.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood’s contributions to the art world were formally recognized through several significant honors.
In 1911, following his work as the official artist for the royal visit to India, King George V appointed George Percy Jacomb-Hood as official artist for the royal visit to India.
This was a substantial honor, placing George Percy Jacomb-Hood in the inner circle of the royal household and acknowledging his skill in capturing moments of national and imperial importance.
The following year, in 1912, George Percy Jacomb-Hood was awarded the Victoria Order of Merit (VM), a dynastic order of knighthood founded by Queen Victoria herself.

The Victoria Order of Merit is given directly by the sovereign to individuals who have rendered exceptionally meritorious service to the Crown in the fields of the arts, science, learning, and literature.
Being named to the Victoria Order of Merit was a singular distinction, reserved for a very small number of people.
Being named to the Victoria Order of Merit cemented George Percy Jacomb-Hood’s status as one of Britain's foremost artists of his generation.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood's career culminated in a long and distinguished exhibition history, with works shown at the Royal Academy from 1879 onwards, a testament to his enduring relevance and the high regard in which his work was held by the establishment.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood had a consistent exhibition record from 1879–1921 at major venues including the Royal Academy, Grosvenor Gallery, and Paris Salon.
The life of George Percy Jacomb-Hood cannot be fully understood without examining his family background.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood's family background provides a fascinating lens through which to view the duality of the "Jacomb-Hood" name and the contrasts between his own artistic pursuits and those of his father.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's father, Robert Jacomb-Hood (1822–1900), was a man of a completely different profession and era.
Robert Jacomb-Hood was a highly respected civil engineer, whose career was defined by the construction of the physical infrastructure of Victorian Britain.
Robert Jacomb-Hood was the eldest son of Robert Jacomb of Bardon Park, Leicestershire.
Robert Jacomb of Bardon Park, Leicestershire, in 1857, inherited the Bardon estate under the stipulation of adding the surname "Hood" to his own, thus becoming Robert Jacomb-Hood.
The act of inheritance and naming established a lineage that would produce two men of great distinction, albeit in vastly different fields.
Robert Jacomb-Hood (the engineer) was born on January 25, 1822, at Riseley, Bedfordshire.
Robert Jacomb-Hood received his initial training as an articled pupil to George Watson Buck of the Manchester and Birmingham Railway in 1841.
Robert Jacomb-Hood's professional life was dedicated to railways, bridges, and ports.
Robert Jacomb-Hood's career culminated in his appointment as Chief Engineer of the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway (LB&SCR) from its formation in 1846 until 1860.
During this period, Robert Jacomb-Hood oversaw the expansion of the LB&SCR, including the crucial agreement to gain access to Victoria Station in 1860.

Robert Jacomb-Hood authored papers on engineering topics, earning him the prestigious Telford Medal in 1858 for "The Arrangement and Construction of Railway Stations" and a Council Premium in 1880 for another paper.
Robert Jacomb-Hood was elected a Member of the Institution of Civil Engineers in 1847.
Robert Jacomb-Hood died suddenly on May 10, 1900, at Tunbridge Wells, aged 78.
The lives of father and son represent two pillars of Victorian society: the engineer who built the nation's transportation network and the artist who captured its social and cultural soul.
The legacy of George Percy Jacomb-Hood is that of a consummate professional and a significant chronicler of his time.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood was a master of the society portrait, a genre that, while often dismissed today, was a major force in the art world of his day.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood's work provides an invaluable visual archive of the British aristocracy and upper-middle class, offering insights into their tastes, personalities, and self-perception during a period of immense social change.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's portraits, characterized by their psychological depth and technical mastery, remain a testament to his skill as a draftsman and observer.
Beyond portraiture, George Percy Jacomb-Hood's extensive body of illustration work, particularly for the works of Oscar Wilde and Andrew Lang, secured his place in the history of book illustration.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's elegant and evocative drawings helped shape the reader's imagination and contributed to the enduring popularity of these classic texts.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's career was a model of dedication to one's craft, combining a rigorous academic training with a deep understanding of the social world he inhabited.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's career was defined by his success within the established channels of the British art world.

Through his membership in prestigious institutions, his official appointments, and his prolific output, George Percy Jacomb-Hood achieved a level of fame and respect that few of his contemporaries could match.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood was a product of the Victorian and Edwardian elite, and his work inevitably reflects the values and hierarchies of that society.
George Percy Jacomb-Hood's artistic skill, his humanist approach, and his ability to infuse traditional subjects with a sense of modernity ensure that his work continues to be valued.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood stands as a bridge between the academic traditions of the past and the more experimental currents of the future, a figure who mastered the conventions of his time while subtly pushing against their boundaries.

The story of George Percy Jacomb-Hood's life, intertwined with the name of his engineer father, serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of careful historical research in disentangling familial legacies and accurately assigning credit where it is due.

1 Fine Victorian Oil Painting Portrait Young Lady Cherry Lips In Blue Dress White Ruff Frilly Collar.  
Subject portrait of a beautiful young lady in half length front profile view facing the viewer in a loving gaze. She is wearing a traditional blue dress with white ruff frilly collar she has thick brown hair, with blue eyes, cherry lips and light skin rose cheeks complexion she is projecting such beauty, elegance in her pose.  
Title " A portrait of a young lady wearing blue dress with white collar"

Oil on panel.

Signed by the known British artist George Percy Jacomb-Hood.  
Biography of the artist George Percy Jacomb-Hood MVO R.B.A (6 July 1857 – 11 December 1929) was a painter, etcher and illustrator. He was a founding member of the New English Art Club and Society of Portrait Painters. Early life- Jacomb-Hood was born on 6 July 1857 at Redhill in Surrey, the fourth of nine children (two of whom died in infancy) of Robert Jacomb-Hood (1822–1900) and Jane Stothard Littlewood (1827–1869). His grandfather, a yeoman farmer in Essex was born Robert Jacomb (1794–1857), but was a cousin of William Hood, the last male member of his family, who left his estate at Bardon, Leicestershire to him on condition that he took the additional surname of Hood, the estate having been in the Hood family since the 1620s. His father was Chief Engineer on the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway from 1846–1860.  
Jacomb-Hood was educated at Tonbridge School and the Slade School of Fine Art as well as studying while touring abroad in Paris and Madrid. He was a member of the Royal Society of Painter-Etchers, the Savile Club, was Honorary Treasurer of the Chelsea Arts Club, member of the New English Art Club and the Royal Society of Portrait Painters. He exhibited at the first exhibition of the Society of Graphic Art in London in 1921. His Career - Jacomb-Hood regularly produced illustrations for The Graphic who gave him a number of overseas assignments.  
In 1896 the magazine sent him to Greece and to Delhi in 1902. He accompanied the Prince and Princess of Waleson their 1905 tour of India and was a member of George V's personal staff on his 1911 tour of India.\[5\] He also painted Madeleine Shaw-Lefevre in her role as principal of Somerville College, Oxford. He wrote an autobiography in 1925, entitled With Brush and Pencil.  
Jacomb-Hood married The Hon Henrietta Kemble de Hochepied-Larpent (1867–1941), daughter of Arthur de Hochepied Larpent, 8th Baron de Hochepied on 28 June 1910.\[7\] On their marriage, John Singer Sargent, a friend and neighbour of Jacomb-Hood's in Chelsea, gave them his watercolour Italian Sailing Vessels at Anchor (c 1904–07) inscribed "to my friend Jacomb Hood" and now at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, presented in 1943 by her sister and heiress. Known as Reta, her sister The Hon Sybil Marguerite Gonne de Hochepied-Larpent, OBE (1867–1941) married Philip Napier Miles and Jacomb-Hood was a friend of his cousin Frank Miles. Another sister, The Hon Clarissa Catherine de Hochepied-Larpent, married the soldier and artist Colonel Robert Charles Goff. The Jacomb-Hoods lived in Chelsea after Frank Miles's death when Jacomb-Hood's father bought Miles's house in Tite Street from his executors and also had a house in Rye, East Sussex. He died on 11 December 1929 at Philip Napier Miles's villa at Alassio in Italy.

Walk into any of the women’s colleges at Oxford, and sooner or later you will encounter the earliest pioneers in women’s higher education, immortalised in paint. These portraits were crowd-funded and commissioned by alumnae groups, staff and students to commemorate history through the ‘portrait transaction’, that is, the negotiation between sitter, maker, conventions and commission.[\[1\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn1) Painted to commemorate the principals, tutors and supporters of these colleges, these portraits were intended as symbols of collective identity, college traditions and institutional continuity.[\[2\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn2)

![Image 1: madeleineshaw lefevre](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/madeleineshaw-lefevre.jpg?itok=SO9xLTtx)

George Percy Jacomb-Hood, Madeleine Shaw-Lefevre, 1890. Oil on canvas, 118 x 89 cm. Gift from the Council and Students, 1890. Somerville College, Oxford.

The earliest paintings indicate the quasi-maternal role played by early college leaders, who were appointed as wardens with administrative and pastoral care duties. Some of these women, such as the first Principal of Lady Margaret Hall, Elizabeth Wordsworth (1840-1932) or the first Principal of Somerville College, Oxford, Madeleine Shaw-Lefevre (1835-1914) had not had a university education themselves.[\[3\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn3) Shaw-Lefevre was appointed in part for her social work, her connections and her credentials as a respectable, cultivated woman, ‘the very antipodes of the clumsy, masculine blue-stocking’, as Wordsworth put it.[\[4\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn4) An alumna of Somerville noted that Shaw-Lefevre’s charm was ‘invaluable in disarming the hostile criticism with which the foundation of a woman’s college in Oxford was greeted from many quarters’.[\[5\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn5) Portraits of this generation of leaders present their sitters as demurely yet finely dressed elegant women, seated within artistic domestic interiors.

![Image 2: elizabethwordsworth](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/elizabethwordsworth.jpg?itok=OU-PVRkp)

James Jebusa Shannon, Dame Elizabeth Wordsworth, 1891. Oil on canvas, 125 x 100 cm. Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford.

George Percy Jacomb-Hood’s Portrait of Madeleine Shaw-Lefevre (1890) and James Jebusa Shannon’s Portrait of Dame Elizabeth Wordsworth (1891) exemplify this trend. In Jacomb-Hood’s portrait, Shaw-Lefevre wears a black satin evening dress, with fur wrap and translucent lace gloves, resting her chin in one hand, books visible on the shelf behind her. Her portrait, completed in eight weeks, after three or four sittings a week, captures a thoughtful grace, inquiring and listening.[\[6\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn6) Wordsworth sits for Shannon in a similarly elegant interior, wearing a grey satin and embroidered tea gown, with a bowl of irises at her elbow. Both Jacomb-Hood and Shannon were renowned society portrait painters, who charged great sums for their sought-after portraits. Both painters were members of the New English Art Club, a group of artists who experimented with French modernism.[\[7\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn7) Loose brushwork brings a shining delicacy to both women’s dresses in these portraits: a conservative approach to their subject is paired with innovative painting technique. These portraits would have been recognisably fashionable in style – and recognisably costly as a financial outlay – to prospective students and their parents, promoting an impression of the college as an elite institution, comparable to the older men’s colleges.

![Image 3: dorotheabeale](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/dorotheabeale.jpg?itok=IIQ2bD6q)

After James Jebusa Shannon, Portrait of Dorothea Beale. Oil on canvas, 124 x 99 cm. St Hilda’s College, Oxford.

Shannon painted a number of portraits for early British women’s colleges in the 1890s, including Royal Holloway College and Newnham College as well as St Hilda’s College, where a copy of his portrait of Dorothea Beale still hangs today.[\[8\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn8) Colleges looked to each other for inspiration when searching for possible artists to undertake these important commissions. Correspondence held at Lady Margaret Hall relating to the search for an artist to paint former principal, Lynda Grier (1880-1967), reflects an earlier practice. In this, the painter was chosen collaboratively by sitter and portrait committee, who relied on the sharing of knowledge across the Oxbridge women’s colleges at meetings of the Association of Headmistresses and Principals, as well as visits to the Royal Academy to assess portraits on display in the annual Summer Exhibition.[\[9\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn9)

![Image 4: charlotteannemoberly](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/charlotteannemoberly.jpg?itok=cUgpIhQj)

Samuel Henry William Llewellyn, Charlotte Anne Moberly. Oil on canvas, 75 x 61 cm. St Hugh’s Hall, Oxford.

The colleges sometimes appointed Academicians to undertake their portraits, such as Samuel Henry William Llewellyn (1858-1941), later the President of the Royal Academy (1928-38), who painted Charlotte Anne Moberly (1846-1937), the first Principal of St Hugh’s Hall.[\[10\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn10) Moberly’s frothy lace sleeves, a delicate pendant and the small posy pinned to her chest soften the severity of her high-necked black dress, wire-rimmed spectacles and simply styled hair. Seated against a painted landscape, Moberly occupies a liminal space, between interior and exterior, the natural world and the artificial, as Llewellyn chooses to play down Moberly’s academic credentials in favour of emphasis on feminine respectability.

![Image 5: clarapater](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/clarapater.jpg?itok=wmjMg1Vh)

Lowes Cato Dickinson, Clara Pater, 1860. Oil on canvas, 80 x 62 cm. Somerville College, Oxford.

In addition to commissioned portraits, the women’s colleges also received and displayed a number of donated portraits, depicting famous students, tutors and founders. In 1896, after Vice Principal Clara Pater (1841-1910) left Somerville for King’s College London, subscribers purchased and presented Lowes Cato Dickinson’s rather girlish portrait of her, which had been painted nearly 40 years earlier.

![Image 6: marysomerville](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/marysomerville.jpg?itok=K9wANk_7)

John Jackson, Mary Somerville as a Young Woman. Oil on canvas, 58 x 47 cm. Somerville College, Oxford.

![Image 7: agnescatherinemaitland](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/agnescatherinemaitland.jpg?itok=4q5lfNfG)

Herbert James Gunn, Agnes Catherine Maitland. Oil on canvas, 90 x 70 cm. Somerville College, Oxford.

The colleges also received gifts from external donors, such as Pre-Raphaelite painter and art dealer Charles Fairfax Murray’s donation of John Jackson’s Mary Somerville as a Young Woman.[\[11\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn11) Murray gave many of his English portraits to the Fitzwilliam Museum, but museum director Sydney Cockerell guided this gift to Somerville in 1911.[\[12\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn12) The portrait is now displayed in an ornate frame, set in the panelling of the college dining hall.

In a sense, the history of women’s college portraits runs parallel to the development of women’s college buildings. Portraits commemorate particular people and eras in college history, but they also function as interior decoration, indicative of colleges’ wealth and status, presenting a quasi ‘gallery of ancestors’ constructed from a uniquely female lineage. On occasion, additions to this lineage were made several years after a subject had left her position at the college. Agnes Maitland (1889-1906), second Principal of Somerville College, died in post in 1906.[\[13\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn13) Her posthumous portrait was undertaken by Herbert James Gunn, who painted her from photographs, and was only given to the college by bequest from Mrs Scoresby Routledge in 1937.[\[14\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn14) Catherine Ouless’s portrait of Esther Burrows, Principal of St Hilda’s College (1893-1910), was only painted in 1927, towards the end of the principalship of Winifred H. Moberly (1919-28), whom Ouless also painted for the college in 1929.[\[15\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn15) Ouless’s small oil sketch for Burrows’ portrait is also held at St Hilda’s today.

![Image 8: estherburrows](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/estherburrows.jpg?itok=R6Ty0_Ou)

Catherine Ouless, Esther Burrows, 1927. Oil on canvas, 70 x 60 cm. St Hilda’s College, Oxford.

![Image 9: winifredhmoberly](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/winifredhmoberly.jpg?itok=9ZZhlrPA)

Catherine Ouless, Winifred H. Moberly, 1929. Oil on canvas, 72 x 57 cm. St Hilda’s College, Oxford.

Catherine Ouless (1879-1961) was unusual among the portrait painters commissioned by the committees and networks associated with the early women’s colleges, which often appointed well-known portraitists who regularly exhibited at the Royal Academy. Ouless herself usually painted landscapes, but she was the eldest daughter of a successful society portrait painter, Walter William Ouless (1848-1933), with whom she occasionally collaborated as a portraitist, for example in their 1925 portrait of Andrew Carnegie (National Galleries Scotland). This may have helped her win the two St Hilda’s commissions.[\[16\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn16)

The contrast between Ouless’s two portraits for the college, of Esther Burrows and Winifred H. Moberly, demonstrate the differences between the first and second generations of leaders at women’s colleges. Burrows’s gentility is emphasised by her delicate lace shawl and jewel at her throat, a three-quarter-profile portrait set in an oval frame. By contrast, Moberly is presented off-centre, clad in her Oxford MA hood, looking assertively at the viewer.

![Image 10: christineburrows](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/christineburrows.jpg?itok=j9FVKDSB)

Unknown artist, Christine Burrows, c. 1920. Oil on canvas, 90 x 70 cm. St Hilda’s College, Oxford.

A portrait of Christine Burrows (1872-1959), Esther’s daughter who held the Principalship following her mother and before Moberly, combines the softness of the former with the assertion of the latter.[\[17\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn17) Wearing a black velvet choker and jewel that seems to be the same one worn by her mother, she is presented in a commanding profile view, holding a book and wearing the crimson hood and gown of the Oxford MA, dating the portrait to after 1920.

![Image 11: henriettajex blake](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/henriettajex-blake.jpg?itok=sagCYQhX)

Philip de László, Henrietta Jex-Blake, 1921. Oil on canvas, 90 x 69.5 cm. Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford.

Principals like Moberly and Christine Burrows had studied at university themselves, but had only recently been granted their degrees and the sartorial regalia associated with those degrees, after Oxford opened degrees to women in October 1920. Prior to this date, women like Emily Penrose (1858-1942), who had studied at Somerville before becoming principal there (1907-26), had opted to receive their degrees from Trinity College Dublin under the ad eundam agreement between the universities.[\[18\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn18) Her [portrait by Philip de László](https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/dame-emily-penrose-18581942-12895/view_as/grid/search/works:dame-emily-penrose-18581942/page/1), painted for Royal Holloway College in 1907, records her appearance wearing Trinity’s distinctive blue hood.[\[19\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn19) This portrait was the first of many De László would paint for the women’s colleges, including a portrait of Lady Margaret Hall’s Principal Henrietta Jex-Blake (1862-1953) wearing her new Oxford MA hood in 1921, and a portrait of Dr A. Maude Royden, a preacher and campaigner for the ordination of women whose portrait was donated to her alma mater, Lady Margaret Hall.[\[20\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn20)

![Image 12: mauderoyden](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_medium/public/owcah/images/media/mauderoyden.jpg?itok=dFaaDhU6)

Philip de László, Dr A. Maude Royden, 1932. Oil on canvas, 132.5 x 98.4 cm. Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford.

De László’s portraits draw on earlier portraiture traditions to present women wearing academic dress in a distinctly feminine manner. Like Emily Penrose, these sitters wear their university hoods askew across the upper body like a sash, or the drapery of neoclassical dress, but if anything they are more feminine in appearance than the statuesque, standing Penrose, recalling more closely the portraits of enlightenment intellectuals from the Bluestockings Circle, such as Robert Edge Pine’s [painting of Catherine MacCaulay, née Sawbridge](https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/catharine-macaulay-nee-sawbridge-157597), or Catherine Read’s [portrait of Elizabeth Carter](https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/elizabeth-carter-17171806-50480/view_as/grid/search/collections:dr-johnsons-house/page/1).[\[21\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn21)

![Image 13: groupportrait](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_large/public/owcah/images/media/groupportrait.jpg?itok=uwGt39gq)

Henry Lamb, Group Portrait, 1936. Oil on canvas, 100 x 120 cm. St Hugh’s College, Oxford.

Just this handful of examples demonstrates how the formal portraits commissioned by the early women’s colleges at Oxford speak to inherent tensions surrounding women’s education in the years before and after women first received their degrees in 1920. In many ways these portraits exemplify the conservatism and caution of the colleges more generally. As Martha Vicinus put it, this caution ‘locked women into a rigid mould of respectability, when they might have gained more by daring more’.[\[22\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn22) Portraits were often commissioned from respected, known artists, whose work was recognisable as a financial investment. These portraits were initially conventional in composition and sitters’ dress, with little to distinguish them from the family portraiture of the day.[\[23\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftn23) Yet later artists such as De László developed new portrait types, which presented these distinguished women wearing academic dress, drawing on neo-classical traditions to recall female figures like the sibyls and the muses, thus rooting a radical subject in respectability. By the 1930s, women wearing academic gowns had become a kind of uniform, as recorded by Henry Taylor Lamb’s Group Portrait of five Fellows of St Hugh’s.

* * *

[\[1\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref1) Joanna Woodall uses the phrase ‘portrait transaction’ in her introduction to Portraiture: Facing the Subject (Manchester, 1997), p. 7. See also Ludmilla J. Jordanova’s expansion on the term: Jordanova, Defining Features: Scientific and Medical Portraits, 1660-2000 (London, 2000), p. 23.

[\[2\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref2) For the role of portraiture at Royal Holloway College and Bedford College, see Imogen Tedbury, Modern Portraits for Modern Women: Principals and Pioneers from the Royal Holloway and Bedford New College Art Collection (Egham, 2020). For alumnae associations as collectors, see Imogen Tedbury, ‘New Collections for New Women: Collecting and Commissioning Portraits at the Early Women’s University Colleges’, 19: Interdisciplinary Studies in the Long Nineteenth Century 2020 (31). (2021). doi: [https://doi.org/10.16995/ntn.3353](https://doi.org/10.16995/ntn.3353)

[\[3\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref3) Enid Huws Jones, ‘Lefevre, Madeleine Septimia Shaw- (1835-1914)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 23 September 2004. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/48463;](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/48463;) Frances Lannon, ‘Worsworth, Dame Elizabeth \[pseud. Grant Lloyd\] (1840-1932)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 23 September 2004. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/37024](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/37024).

[\[4\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref4) Elizabeth Wordsworth, ‘Miss M. Shaw Lefevre’, Oxford Magazine (16 Oct 1914), 5-6, p. 5.

[\[5\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref5) Vera Farnell, A Somervillian Looks Back (Oxford, 1948), p. 8.

[\[6\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref6) Farnell, A Somervillian, p. 7.

[\[7\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref7) Kenneth McConkey, The New English: A History of the New English Art Club (London, 2006).

[\[8\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref8) For Shannon’s other portraits of female educators, see Tedbury, ‘New Collections’, 5-12.

[\[9\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref9) These practises are indicated through correspondence regarding Lady Margaret Hall’s portrait of principal Lynda Grier. On 23 September 1952, principal Lucy Sutherland wrote to former principal Grier that she had been to the Royal Academy ‘to get a few ideas’. On 30 September 1952, she wrote that When I was up at the meeting of Headmistresses and Principals the Cambridge people happened to mention that \[Rodrigo\] Moynihan had done what they considered a very poor portrait of the late Mistress of Girton.’ Domestic Papers Box 3, Portraits, LSS file. Lady Margaret Hall Archives.

[\[10\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref10) Janet Howarth, ‘Moberly, Charlotte Anne Elizabeth \[Annie\] (1846-1937), Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 23 September 2004. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/48453](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/48453).

[\[11\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref11) John Jackson (1778-1831) was a prolific portraitist working in the tradition of Sir Thomas Lawrence and Henry Raeburn, elected to the Royal Academy in 1817.

[\[12\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref12) Paul Tucker, ‘Customer, Counsel, Associate, “Trustee”: Charles Fairfax Murray and Thomas Agnew and Sons (1886-1918)’, in Lynne Catterson (ed.), Florence, Berlin and Beyond: Late Nineteenth-Century Art Market and Their Social Networks (Leiden: Brill, 2019), pp. 209-48, p. 244.

[\[13\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref13) Enid Huws Jones, ‘Maitland, Agnes Catherine (1849-1906), Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 23 September 2014. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/34836](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/34836).

[\[14\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref14) Herbert James Gunn (1893-1964) was a Royal Academician who, like James Jebusa Shannon and Philip de László, became a real favourite to undertake portrait commissions for the early women’s colleges, perhaps because of his relatively conservative style. See Tedbury, Modern Portraits, p. 14, p. 52.

[\[15\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref15) Margaret E. Rayner, ‘Burrows \[née Bliss\], Esther Elizabeth (1847-1935), Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 23 September 2004. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/48432;](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/48432;) Margaret E. Rayner, ‘Moberly, Winifred Horsbrugh (1875-1928)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 23 September 2004. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/48456](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/48456).

[\[16\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref16) For Ouless and her father, see Philip Stevens, Dictionary of Painters of the Channel Islands (Jersey, 2002).

[\[17\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref17) R. F. Butler, revised by Margaret E. Rayner, ‘Burrows, Christine Mary Elizabeth (1872-1959), Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 08 October 2009. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/32198](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/32198).

[\[18\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref18) S. M. Parkes, ‘Steamboat ladies’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 4 October 2007. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/61643;](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/61643;) Pauline Adams, ‘Penrose, Dame Emily (1858-1942)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 23 September 2004.  [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/35466;](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/35466;) Pauline Adams, Somerville for Women: An Oxford College, 1879-1993 (Oxford, 1996).

[\[19\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref19) For this portrait, see Tedbury, Modern Portraits, pp. 56-60.

[\[20\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref20) Sheila Fletcher, ‘Royden, (Agnes) Maude (1876-1956)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 23 September 2004. [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/35861](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/35861).

[\[21\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref21) See Tedbury, ‘Modern Collections’, p. 25.

[\[22\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref22) Martha Vicinus, Independent Women: Work and Community for Single Women: 1850-1920 (London, 1985), p. 136.

[\[23\]](https://www.firstwomenatoxford.ox.ac.uk/article/painting-the-pioneers-portraits-of-women-at-oxford#_ftnref23) Deborah Cherry made a similar remark about Rudolph Lehman’s portrait of Emily Davies, presented to Girton College in 1880. Cherry, Beyond the Frame, p. 197.

  George Percy Jacomb-Hood

  An Episode in the Life of the Duke of Alva

    George Percy Jacomb-Hood, the late 19th century
	British painter, illustrator and etcher created this original grisaille painting entitled, "An Episode in the Life
	of the Duke of Alva"  for a novel entitled, My Lady of Orange  by the British author, Henry
	Christopher Bailey (H. C. Bailey), published in 1901 by Longmans, Green, and Company. It is painted on thin board
	with full margins and signed in the lower left corner with George Percy Jacomb-Hood's characteristic monogramme.
      The Duke of Alva (Fernando Alvarez de Toledo, 1508 - 1582), is best remembered
	  for his tyrannical government of the Netherlands from 1567 to 1573. Appointed by King Philip II of Spain,
          the Duke of Alva was sent to Holland to squash those who had revolted
          against Spanish rule. Blessed by the Pope and with the full authority
          of the Inquisition Alva carried out his objectives with both cruelty
      and swiftness.

      Title:
    An Episode in the Life of the Duke of Alva

      Artist:
    Jacomb-Hood, George Percy (Redhill, Surrey, 1857 -
      Chelsea, 1929)

      Date:
    c. 1900 - 1901

      Medium:
    Original Grisaille Painting

      Note:
    George Percy Jacomb-Hood: A major English
      painter, illustrator and etcher, George Percy Jacomb-Hood (also spelt, 'Jacombe-Hood')
      first studied at the Slade School of Art, London, under both Alphonse Legros
      and Edward Poynter. He then concluded his studies under J. P. Laurens, in
      Paris. G. P. Jacomb-Hood began exhibiting his paintings at the Royal Academy,
      London, as early as 1879. During the following decades he also exhibited
      his art at the Grosvenor Gallery, the Paris Salon and the Royal Society
      of British Artists. He was a founding member of the New English Art Club
      and the Society of Portrait Painters and a full member of the Royal Institute
      of Oil Painters and the Royal Society of British Artists. In 1911, King George
      V selected George Percy Jacomb-Hood as his official artist for his visit to India. In
      the following year he was also awarded the Victoria Order of Merit.

    Today the paintings, drawings and etchings of George Percy
      Jacomb-Hood are found in the following collections; the Bristol Art Gallery,
      Manchester Art Gallery, Victoria Hall, Calcutta, India, the Victoria and
      Albert Museum, London, the National Portrait Gallery, London, de Young Museum,
      San Francisco, and the Library of Congress, Washington, DC.

    George Percy Jacomb-Hood was equally adept as a painter of portraits, mythological
      subjects, genre scenes and figure studies. These talents kept him regularly
      employed as a leading illustrator. In this capacity he was frequently commissioned
      by major illustrated journals, particularly The Graphic and the Illustrated
      London News. More importantly he illustrated a number of great turn-of-the-century
      books. These include, P. G. Hamerton's, Paris in Old and Present Times
      (1885), Andrew Lang's, Auccassin and Nicolette (1887), The
      Blue Fairy Book (1889) and The History of Whittington and other
      Stories (1904), J. M. Strachey's Nursery Lyrics (1893) and
      Oscar Wilde's, The Happy Prince and other Tales (1888).

    At the turn of the century, George Percy Jacomb-Hood was commissioned to
      illustrate two historical romance novels which both had as their settings
      16th century Holland during the turbulent era of the Inquisition. These
      novels were H. C. Bailey's, My Lady of Orange and H. Rider Haggard's,
      Lisbeth, A Tale of the Dutch. Both books were published by Longmans,
      Green & Co. in London in 1901. It is likely that this original grisaille
      painting was meant as an illustration for My Lady of Orange, as
      this novel deals with a fictional Englishman who joins William of Orange
      in opposing the Duke of Alva. The Duke of Alva (Fernando Alvarez de Toledo,
      1508 - 1582), of course, is regrettably not a fictional character. He is
      best remembered for his tyrannical government of the Netherlands from 1567
      to 1573. Appointed by King Philip II of Spain, the Duke of Alva was sent to Holland
      to squash those who had revolted against Spanish rule. Blessed by the Pope
      and with the full authority of the Inquisition Alva carried out his objectives
      with both cruelty and swiftness. In fact he once boasted that during his
      six year reign he had executed over 18,000 men. Obviously these were most
      dangerous times. Thus the person in this painting is probably an escaping
      noble who wears the cloak as a disguise.

    An Episode in the Life of the Duke of Alva clearly
      shows George Jacomb-Hood's gifts as a historical painter and illustrator. Using
      the demanding gray monochrome medium of grisaille painting he has created
      a brilliant image of strong tonal values and of light and shade. The original
      art gallery sticker for this important painting has been preserved and accompanies
      this work of art.

    George Percy Jacomb Hood's original grisaille painting entitled,
	 An Episode in the Life of the Duke of Alva was created for a novel entitled, My Lady of Orange
      by the English author, Henry Christopher Bailey (1878-1961) published in 1901 by Longmans, Green, and Co., containing eight
	  illustrated plates. According to the Rue Morgue Press and other sources, My Lady of Orange was H. C. Bailey's first novel, published while
	  he was still a student at Oxford. Although Bailey authored many books and was a prolific writer in many fields throughout
	  his career, such as Karl of Erbach (1903), The Lonely Lady (1911), The
	  Young Lovers (1917) and many others, he was most famous for his mystery and detective stories such as
	  Mr. Fortune's Practice (1920), Mr. Fortune Speaking (1929, The Wrong Man (1944),
	  Honour Among Thieves (1947). These latter included his famous characters, Mr. Reggie Fortune, a doctor
	  turned detective and Joshua Clunk a course, Hymn-quoting attorney, which Baley included in many other detective novels.

      Size:
    12 3/8 X 9 5/8 (Sizes in inches are approximate, height
      preceding width of plate-mark or image.)

      Framed and Matted with 100% Archival Materials

      View larger Framed Image

      Buy Now
      Price: $1,395.00 US

      Condition:
    Painted on thin board and with full margins. Signed in the
      lower left corner with Jacomb-Hood's characteristic monogramme. Containing
      several faint scuff marks along the upper margin else in very good condition
      throughout without a sign of fading or discolouration. An Episode in
      the Life of the Duke of Alva stands as a prime, original example of
      the famous art of G. P. Jacomb-Hood.

A History of the Royal Society of Portrait Painters
===================================================

You are here:

1.  [Home](https://therp.co.uk/ "Home")
2.  [ARCHIVE](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/ "ARCHIVE")
3.  A History of the Royal…

![Image 3: Detail of Lord Elphinstone by Philip de Laszlo Member of the Royal Society of Portrait Painters](https://therp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Detail-de-Laszlo-Elphinstone-234x300.jpg)Detail of Lord Elphinstone by Philip de Laszlo Member of the Royal Society of Portrait Painters

During the last quarter of the 19th century, interest in portrait painting revived. It not only became fashionable to commission portraits as a means of celebrating and honouring those of high rank or achievement, but it was becoming a genre worthy of critical attention.

The Royal Academy, however, remained closed to portraits by those beyond its doors and consequently, a number of young painters banded together, ‘the front rank of Outsiders’ as the _Magazine of Art_ called them, to form their own movement.

**1891** A committee comprising Archibald John Stuart-Wortley (chairman), James Jebusa Shannon, George Percy Jacomb-Hood, Arthur Melville, and Hon. John Collier carried a proposal to form a Society of Portrait Painters. Wortley was its first President and its first exhibition was deemed a critical success.

The catalogue of the exhibition shows that its committee then consisted of Archibald Stuart-Wortley (Chairman), Hon. John Collier, Arthur Hacker, G. P. Jacomb-Hood, S.J. Solomon, James Jebusa Shannon, and Hubert Vos. The other members listed were Percy Bigland, C. A. Furse, Glazebrook, John McLure Hamilton, Heywood Hardy, Hubert von Herkomer, Henry J. Hudson, Louise Jopling, T. B. Kennington, W. Llewellyn, W. M. Loudan, Arthur Melville, Anna Lea Merritt, F. M. Skipworth, Mrs. Annie Swynnerton, W. R. Symonds, Mary Waller, Edwin A. Ward, Leslie Ward (better known as “Spy”), and T. Blake Wirgman.

**1892** The second exhibition was considered to surpass the first with works by John Everett Millais, Frederick Leighton, and members of the Glasgow School, John Lavery, and James Guthrie.

G F Watts, Alma Tadema, and James McNeill Whistler were made members.

[![Image 4: The cover of Studio Magazine 1945 with an article by Herbert A Oliver about the history of the Royal Society of Portrait Painters](https://therp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Studio-Magazine-1-copy-230x300.jpg)](https://therp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Studio-Magazine-1.pdf)Click to download pdf of Studio Magazine 1945 article on the Royal Society of Portrait Painters

**1893** John Singer Sargent was established at the forefront of their rank. An annual exhibition launched in the newly opened Grafton Galleries in New Bond St.

**1902** The Athenaeum magazine wrote ‘_the mere fact that Mr. Watts contributes some of the work of his prime, raises the exhibition above the ordinary level of contemporary shows’_

**1911** In its 21st year the society gained Royal patronage from King George V, becoming the Royal Society of Portrait Painters (RP). A new wave of painters joined including William Orpen, who broke with past conventions and sought new forms of expression.

**1917** The Society put on an exhibition at the Walker Gallery in Liverpool to raise funds for the war effort.

**1920** The Grafton Gallery lease expired and the RP moved between the Royal Academy and the R.B.A Galleries for some years before finding a permanent home at The Royal Institute Galleries in Piccadilly, until these were bombed in 1940.

**1923** The President and founding member, J.J. Shannon died and was replaced by William Orpen, a President remembered for his magnanimity in instantly writing a cheque to settle the Society’s debts. Orpen was replaced on his death by Lavery, in 1931. During the years that followed such luminaries as Laura Knight, Augustus John, Alfred Munnings among others became members and exhibited with the Society, innovating and propelling it in new directions.

![Image 5: H M The Queen by Antony Williams RP. Winner of the Ondaatje Prize for Portraiture, Royal Society of Portrait Painters 1995](https://therp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/H-M-The-Queen-by-Antony-Williams-RP.-Winner-of-the-Ondaatje-Prize-for-Portraiture-Royal-Society-of-Portrait-Painters-1995-227x300.jpg)H M The Queen by Antony Williams RP. Winner of the Ondaatje Prize for Portraiture, Royal Society of Portrait Painters 1995

**1941** The Society announced a permanent Gallery at  6 ½, Suffolk St, Pall Mall East, London SW1, where the painters’ work could be seen at any time of year

**1961** The RP became a founder member of the [**Federation of British Artists (FBA)**](https://www.mallgalleries.org.uk/about-us)

**1971** The FBA moves to the [Mall Galleries](https://www.mallgalleries.org.uk/) in London

**1984** It was announced by the society _‘The President and members have the honour to announce that Her Majesty the Queen has been graciously pleased to grant Her Patronage to the Royal Society of Portrait Painters.’_

**1986-7** The RP was incorporated as a private limited company and also became a Registered Charity, overseen by John Walton RP.

#Prizewinner:![Image 38](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)![Image 39](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)Today we share the last of our RP Drawing Prize winners who won the Almenara Residency Prize (Awarded to an exhibitor who shows distinctive promise and in the opinion of the jurors will benefit from this residential opportunity) David Jamieson who kindly answered some questions around their exhibiting drawing... CONGRATULATIONS! ![Image 40](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)![Image 41](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)Q. How long did your portrait take to make? Is there anything about the process you’d like to share?![Image 42](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)![Image 43](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)It’s always difficult to be precise about how long I spend on a drawing since I don’t keep careful track of the hours I spend in the studio. But I can give you a time frame of about 6 months, from August 2024 to January 2025, between starting and completing the portrait. During that time, it was on and off my easel with varying frequency, depending on other deadlines, which is why a strict tally of hours is hard to estimate.![Image 44](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)![Image 45](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)Regarding process, this piece was a bit of an experiment in using ink wash to tone paper by hand–a new experience for me. For this kind of drawing, where I use graphite and white pastel to describe form, I like to work on surfaces of a particular value, somewhere between 6 and 7 on the Munsell scale. I find this kind of ground makes for a good ratio of pastel to graphite, or what’s lighter than the paper vs. what’s darker. As it turns out, getting just the right value, color and consistency of tone with ink wash is a bit tricky, requiring much trial and error. I went through several sheets of paper before getting the surface I wanted.![Image 46](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)(...)![Image 47](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)![Image 48](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)\-You can go to the 'NEWS' section of our website for the full interview (or via the link in our bio): [www.therp.co.uk](https://www.therp.co.uk/)![Image 49](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)And our Drawing Prize exhibition may be closed but you can still view it online as well as many drawings being available to purchase!![Image 50](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)![Image 51](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)Image: David Jamieson, '‘Pathologist – Portrait of Dr Maurice Jamieson’ ![Image 52](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)@vitruvianstudio![Image 53](https://therp.co.uk/portrait-archive/a-history-of-the-royal-society-of-portrait-painters/)@almenaracollection ... 0what%E2%80%99s%20darker.%20As%20it%20turns%20out%2C%20getting%20just%20the%20right%20value%2C%20color%20and%20consistency%20of%20tone%20with%20ink%20wash%20is%20a%20bit%20tricky%2C%20requiring%20much%20trial%20and%20error.%20I%20went%20through%20several%20sheets%20of%20paper%20before%20getting%20the%20surface%20I%20wanted.%28...%29-You%20can%20go%20to%20the%20%26%23039%3BNEWS%26%23039%3B%20section%20of%20our%20website%20for%20the%20full%20interview%20%28or%20via%20the%20link%20in%20our%20bio%29%3A%20www.therp.co.ukAnd%20our%20Drawing%20Prize%20exhibition%20may%20be%20closed%20but%20you%20can%20still%20view%20it%20online%20as%20well%20as%20many%20drawings%20being%20available%20to%20purchase%21Image%3A%20David%20Jamieson%2C%20%26%23039%3B%E2%80%98Pathologist%20%E2%80%93%20Portrait%20of%20Dr%20Maurice%20Jamieson%E2%80%99%20%40vitruvianstudio%40almenaracollection%09%09%09%09)
